Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette:
Margaret had spent most of her adult life on the water, and even in her seventies she still spoke about the deck, the engines, and the weather with the steady authority of someone who had built her identity around command. Widowed and living alone, she continued working as a ship captain because, as she put it, “there is always something to do out there.” It was on a late evening docking in a busy port that her life shifted. During a dispute with law enforcement on the pier, police officers used force against her in a way she experienced as sudden, humiliating, and terrifying. She had not expected to be handled that way, and what stayed with her was not only the physical roughness but the shock of being treated as if she were dangerous. In the months that followed, she found herself returning again and again to that scene, not in a vague way but in exact fragments that came back with startling clarity. She could picture the lights, the positions of the officers, the angle of her own body, and the expression on one officer’s face. When she described it, she did so as though she were reading from an image already developed in her mind; she said it was “like looking at photographs,” one after another, fixed and detailed, impossible to blur or soften.

At first Margaret tried to carry on as before, telling herself that the incident was behind her and that a woman who had spent a lifetime at sea should not be undone by one night on shore. Yet when the memory surfaced, it did not feel like something safely past. She would be standing in her cabin or reviewing paperwork in the ship’s office and suddenly feel herself back on the pier, with the force of the encounter arriving so vividly that it seemed to be happening again in the present tense. She did not describe this as a distant recollection; rather, she said that when she remembered it, she felt as if she were “right there again,” her body bracing as if the officers were still in front of her. The memory carried a sensory precision that made it difficult for her to separate then from now, and that was especially disorienting for a woman who had always trusted her ability to assess danger quickly and accurately. What upset her most was not only what had happened, but how unmistakably real it remained.

Over time, Margaret began to organize her days around staying occupied. She threw herself into work with a determination that those around her noticed. On the ship she would take on extra tasks, check details that others could have handled, and keep moving from one responsibility to the next long after most of the crew had gone off duty. In the office she lingered over administrative work, finding that the routine of schedules, logs, and maintenance lists gave her something solid to grip when her thoughts started to drift back to the incident. She preferred being busy to sitting still, and she came to dread unstructured moments because they left room for the memory to intrude. At the same time, she found herself going over and over why it had happened to her. She searched for meaning in the encounter, turning it over in her mind with a kind of exhausted insistence. Why her, after all these years? Why had it happened in the middle of an ordinary work night, when she had done nothing to invite it? The questions did not lead anywhere satisfying, but she could not seem to leave them alone.

She also dwelled on the version of herself she had been before the event. Margaret spoke with visible grief about the woman she used to be: more self-assured, more willing to move through a port or a crowded dock without calculating every interaction, less preoccupied with being taken by surprise. She noticed that she had become less easy in her own skin, though she still dressed and worked with her customary neatness. The contrast between who she had been and who she felt herself to be now weighed on her, especially because she had built a life around competence and independence. In recent weeks, she sought help because the memories were no longer something she could simply outwork or reason through alone. She worried that if she kept pushing herself to stay occupied, she would never feel fully present again, yet she was equally frightened by the force with which the event returned whenever she slowed down. What she most hoped for was to be able to remember the incident without being pulled back into it, and what she most feared was that the clarity of those images would keep stealing the life and steadiness she had spent decades at sea learning to protect.
